metadata.title: Left-invariant Grauert Tubes on $SU(2)$
metadata.authors: Vaqaas Aslam, Daniel M Burns Jr., Daniel Irvine

nodes.name: Entirety of the Grauert tube of a left-invariant metric
nodes.statement: We try to address here the question of whether a left-invariant metric has an entire Grauert tube.
nodes.statement_short: Decide which left-invariant metrics on a compact Lie group have an entire Grauert tube.

nodes.name: Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke necessary condition for an entire tube
nodes.statement: Lempert and Sz\H{o}ke \cite{ls} have shown that a necessary condition for the tube of $(M, g)$ to be entire is that the sectional curvatures of $g$ be non-negative.
nodes.statement_short: Non-negative sectional curvature is necessary for the Grauert tube to be entire.
assumptions: the tube of $(M, g)$ to be entire
conclusions: the sectional curvatures of $g$ be non-negative

nodes.name: Sz\H{o}ke's two-parameter family of metrics of revolution on $S^2$
nodes.statement: Sz\H{o}ke has shown that there is only a two parameter family of metrics of revolution on $S^2$ which have entire tubes, whereas many of these manifolds have strictly positive curvature.
nodes.statement_short: Only a 2-parameter family of rotationally symmetric metrics on $S^2$ has entire tubes.
assumptions: metrics of revolution on $S^2$
conclusions: there is only a two parameter family of metrics of revolution on $S^2$ which have entire tubes

nodes.name: Aguilar's higher-order conditions for entire tubes
nodes.statement: Furthermore, for $M$ of two dimensions, Aguilar \cite{a2} has found an infinite sequence of conditions generalizing that of Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke to higher order invariants which give necessary and sufficient conditions that a tube be entire.
nodes.statement_short: In dimension 2 an infinite sequence of higher-order invariant conditions characterizes entire tubes.
assumptions: for $M$ of two dimensions
conclusions: an infinite sequence of conditions generalizing that of Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke to higher order invariants which give necessary and sufficient conditions that a tube be entire

nodes.name: Are Aguilar's conditions effectively finite?
nodes.statement: In particular, it is not known whether the conditions are effectively finite, i.e., are redundant after a certain degree.

nodes.name: Sz\H{o}ke: bi-invariant metrics have entire tube equal to $G_{\c}$
nodes.statement: If the metric $g$ is bi-invariant on $G$, then Sz\H{o}ke \cite{s} has shown that the tube is entire and equal to $G_{\c}$.
assumptions: the metric $g$ is bi-invariant on $G$
conclusions: the tube is entire and equal to $G_{\c}$

nodes.name: Left-invariant metrics on $S^3$ with $R<0$ have no entire tube
nodes.statement: On the other hand, it is well-known that some left-invariant metrics on $S^3 = SU(2)$ have scalar curvature $R < 0$, which shows they cannot have entire tubes, by Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke's condition.
nodes.statement_short: Some left-invariant metrics on $SU(2)$ have negative scalar curvature, so their tubes cannot be entire.
assumptions: some left-invariant metrics on $S^3 = SU(2)$ have scalar curvature $R < 0$
conclusions: they cannot have entire tubes, by Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke's condition

nodes.name: Arnol'd's observation: geodesic flow equals free rigid body motion
nodes.statement: It is a well-known observation of Arnol'd that the geodesic flow for a left-invariant metric on a compact Lie group is equivalent to the motion of a free rigid body whose frame is parametrized by $G$ about its center of mass (see \cite{via}, Appendix 2, for example).
nodes.statement_short: Left-invariant geodesic flow on a compact Lie group is the same as free rigid-body rotation.
nodes.origin_citation: Arnol'd, Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics, Appendix 2
assumptions: the geodesic flow for a left-invariant metric on a compact Lie group
conclusions: is equivalent to the motion of a free rigid body whose frame is parametrized by $G$ about its center of mass

nodes.name: Generic left-invariant metrics: $Exp_{\c}$ not defined on all of $iTG$
nodes.statement: For a generic left-invariant metric one can show, using the mechanical integrals of motion, that the map $Exp_{\c}$ is not well-defined on all of $i TG$ because most complexified (real) geodesics are not given by entire functions into $G_{\c}$.
nodes.statement_short: For generic left-invariant metrics most complexified geodesics fail to be entire, so $Exp_{\c}$ is not globally defined.
assumptions: For a generic left-invariant metric
conclusions: the map $Exp_{\c}$ is not well-defined on all of $i TG$ because most complexified (real) geodesics are not given by entire functions into $G_{\c}$

nodes.name: Canonical one-form $\Theta$ on $TM$
nodes.statement: Let $\pi: TM \to M$ denote the projection, and let $\Theta$ denote the canonical one-form on $TM$ given by \[ \Theta(V) := (D\pi(V), v), \] where $v \in T_{\pi(v)}M, V \in T_v(TM)$, and $(\cdot,\cdot)$ denotes the Riemannian metric $g$.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas

nodes.name: Adapted complex structure
nodes.statement: An {\em adapted complex structure} on $T^RM := \{v \in TM \, | \, |v| < R\}$ is a complex structure for which the leaves of the Riemann foliation $\mathcal{F}$ of $TM \setminus 0_M$ are complex submanifolds.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas
differentia: the leaves of the Riemann foliation $\mathcal{F}$ of $TM \setminus 0_M$ are complex submanifolds

nodes.name: Riemann foliation
nodes.statement: Recall that the Riemann foliation is given by the tangent sub-bundles to all geodesics for the metric $g$ as leaves.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas
differentia: given by the tangent sub-bundles to all geodesics for the metric $g$ as leaves

nodes.name: Adapted complex structure on $T\r$
nodes.statement: Thus, the adapted complex structure on $T\r$ identifies it with $\c$ via \[ T\r \ni (s, t \frac{d\,\,}{ds}) \to s+ i t \in \c, \] and is functorial for geodesic immersions.
nodes.statement_short: On the tangent bundle of a line the adapted structure is just $s+it \in \c$.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas

nodes.name: Grauert tube; entire tube
nodes.statement: For the maximal radius $R$ for which the adapted complex structure is defined, the complex manifold $T^RM$ is called the {\em Grauert tube} of $(M, g)$. If $R = +\infty$, we say the tube is {\em entire}.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas
differentia: the maximal radius $R$ for which the adapted complex structure is defined

nodes.name: Isometries act holomorphically on the Grauert tube
nodes.statement: If $\phi$ is an isometry of $(M, g)$, then its action by its differential $D\phi$ on the Grauert tube $T^RM$ is holomorphic for the adapted complex structure, while the map $v \to -v$ is anti-holomorphic.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas
assumptions: $\phi$ is an isometry of $(M, g)$
conclusions: its action by its differential $D\phi$ on the Grauert tube $T^RM$ is holomorphic for the adapted complex structure
the map $v \to -v$ is anti-holomorphic

nodes.name: $r^2$ is strictly plurisubharmonic on the tube
nodes.statement: The function $r^2 := |v|^2$ given by the $g$-length squared of vectors is strictly plurisubharmonic on the tube.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas
assumptions: The function $r^2 := |v|^2$ given by the $g$-length squared of vectors
conclusions: is strictly plurisubharmonic on the tube

nodes.name: Liouville form and K\"ahler structure on the tube
nodes.statement: We have that \begin{equation} \frac{i}2 \partial \bar{\partial} r^2 = d\Theta := \Omega \end{equation} is the Liouville form on $TM$ and is a K\"ahler form. The corresponding K\"ahler metric induces the original metric $g$ along the zero section $M$.
nodes.statement_short: $\frac{i}{2}\partial\bar\partial r^2$ is the Liouville K\"ahler form, restricting to $g$ on the zero section.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas
conclusions: \frac{i}2 \partial \bar{\partial} r^2 = d\Theta := \Omega
The corresponding K\"ahler metric induces the original metric $g$ along the zero section $M$

nodes.name: $r$ solves the homogeneous complex Monge-Amp\`ere equation
nodes.statement: $r$ satisfies the homogeneous complex Monge-Amp\`ere equation $\partial \bar{\partial} u^n = 0$ on $T^RM \setminus M$.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas
conclusions: $r$ satisfies the homogeneous complex Monge-Amp\`ere equation $\partial \bar{\partial} u^n = 0$ on $T^RM \setminus M$

nodes.name: Induced vectorfield $\tilde{\xi}$ on $TM$
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be the isometry group of $(M, g)$, and $\mathfrak{g}$ its Lie algebra. An element $\xi \in \mathfrak{g}$ will be identified with its induced vectorfield on $M$. For any vectorfield $\xi$ we will denote by $\Phi^{\xi}_t$ the corresponding 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms. This group lifts to an action by differentials on $TM$, and the induced vectorfield on $TM$ will be denoted $\tilde{\xi}$. In particular, $D\pi\tilde{\xi} = \xi$.
nodes.statement_short: Each Killing field $\xi$ lifts by differentials to a vectorfield $\tilde\xi$ on $TM$ projecting back to $\xi$.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas

nodes.name: Coordinate expression for $\tilde{\xi}$
nodes.statement: If $(q^1, \ldots, q^n)$ are local coordinates on $M$, and $\xi = \sum_k a^k(q) \frac{\partial \,\,}{\partial q^k},$ then in the corresponding coordinates $(q^1, \ldots, q^n, v^1, \ldots, v^n)$ the field $\tilde{\xi}$ can be expressed as follows: \[ \tilde{\xi} = \sum_k a^k(q) \frac{\partial \,\,}{\partial q^k} - \left(\sum_ j v^i \frac{\partial a^k(q)}{\partial q^i}\right) \frac{\partial \,\,}{\partial v^k}. \]
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas

nodes.name: Scale invariance of $\tilde{\xi}$ under $N_{\rho}$
nodes.statement: It will be important to note that \begin{equation} (N_{\rho})_* \, \tilde{\xi} = \tilde{\xi}, \end{equation} for all $\rho \neq 0.$
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas

nodes.name: Holomorphic vectorfield $\tilde{\xi}^{1,0}$ on the tube
nodes.statement: It follows from the property (1) above for Grauert tubes that $\Phi^{\tilde{\xi}}_t$ acts biholomorphically on the tube, and thus \[ \tilde{\xi}^{1,0} = \frac12 (\tilde{\xi} - i J \tilde{\xi}) \] is a holomorphic vectorfield on the tube, where $J$ is the almost complex structure on the tube.
nodes.statement_short: The $(1,0)$-part $\frac12(\tilde\xi - iJ\tilde\xi)$ of a lifted Killing field is holomorphic on the tube.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas

nodes.name: Sz\H{o}ke: $G_{\c}$ acts holomorphically on an entire tube
nodes.statement: Let $(M, g)$ be a compact Riemannian manifold with entire Grauert tube. Then the complex group $G_{\c}$ acts holomorphically on all of the tube, i.e., on all of $TM$ with the adapted complex structure.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas
assumptions: Let $(M, g)$ be a compact Riemannian manifold with entire Grauert tube
conclusions: the complex group $G_{\c}$ acts holomorphically on all of the tube, i.e., on all of $TM$ with the adapted complex structure

nodes.name: Entire tube of a left-invariant metric is biholomorphic to $G_{\c}$
nodes.statement: Let $M = G,$ a compact, connected Lie group, and $g$ be a left invariant metric on $M$. Assume that the Grauert tube of $M$ is entire. Then the connected complex group $G_{\c}$ acts simply transitively on $M_{\c} := TM$, i.e., the entire tube $TM$ is biholomorphic to $G_{\c}$.
nodes.statement_short: If a left-invariant metric on a compact group has an entire tube, that tube is $G_{\c}$.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas
assumptions: Let $M = G,$ a compact, connected Lie group, and $g$ be a left invariant metric on $M$
Assume that the Grauert tube of $M$ is entire
conclusions: the connected complex group $G_{\c}$ acts simply transitively on $M_{\c} := TM$, i.e., the entire tube $TM$ is biholomorphic to $G_{\c}$

nodes.name: Proof that $G_{\c}$ acts simply transitively on the entire tube
nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lemma:action}, we know that $G_{\c}$ acts on $M_{\c}$. We will prove that it acts locally transitively at every point $v \in M_{\c}$. Assuming this for the moment, this proves that all orbits of $G_{\c}$ on $M_{\c}$ are open, and since $M_{\c}$ is connected, this proves that the mapping $A_v: G_{\c} \ni h \to h\cdot v \in M_{\c}$, for any fixed $v \in M_{\c}$, is surjective. Since $G_{\c}, M_{\c}$ are of the same complex dimension, and the map $A_v$ is $G_{\c}$ equivariant, Sard's theorem says that every point in $M_{\c}$ is a regular value of $A_v$, and hence, $A_v$ is a topological covering. If $v \in M$, the covering $A_v: G \to M$ is a diffeomorphism. Since the inclusions $G \subset G_{\c}, M \subset M_{\c}$ are homotopy equivalences, the covering $A_v$ has degree 1 over all of $M_{\c}$, and therefore $A_v$ is a global biholomorphism. \vs \vs To show that $G_{\c}$ acts locally transitively, it suffices to show that \[ DA_{v}: T^{1,0}_{I} G_{\c} = \mathfrak{g}_{\c} \to T_v^{1,0} M_{\c} \] is an isomorphism. This, in turn is equivalent to showing that, for a basis $\xi_1, \xi_2,\ldots, \xi_n$ of $\mathfrak{g}$ over $\r$, the complex fields $\tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_1, \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_2, \ldots, \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_n$ are a basis for $T^{1,0}M_{\c}$ over $\c$ at $v$. Define $\mcp = \{ \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_1 \wedge \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_2 \wedge \ldots \wedge \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_n = 0\}$. We wish to show $\mcp$ is empty. \vs Assume it is not empty. Then $\mcp$ is a $G_{\c}$-invariant divisor on $M_{\c}$, and $\mcp \cap M = \emptyset$. Consider the plurisubharmonic function $u$ restricted to $\mcp$. Since $u$ is non-negative and proper when restricted to $\mcp$, it achieves a global minimum at some $v \in \mcp$. The map $A_v$ restricted to $G$ gives an embedding of $G$ into $\mcp \subset M_{\c}$ where it is a $CR$-submanifold of real dimension $n$. Note that the function $u$ is constant on $S_v := A_v(G)$. Since $\dim_{\c} \mcp < n$, $S_v$ cannot be a totally real submanifold in $\mcp$. Hence its complex tangent space is positive dimensional at every point. Its Levi-form cannot be trivial, since otherwise the leaves of the Levi foliation of $S_v$ would give positive-dimensional complex submanifolds in the level set $\{u = u(v)\}$, which is strictly pseudoconvex, by the tube construction. By a classical construction in complex analysis (local Bishop disks), there exists a continuous mapping $F: \bar{\triangle} \to U \subset M_{\c}$, where $U$ is a small polydisk neighborhood of $v$, and with $F|_{\triangle}$ holomorphic and non-constant, and $F(\partial \triangle) \subset S_v$. Thus $u\circ F|_{\partial\triangle} \equiv u(v)$. Therefore, $F(\triangle) \subset \mcp \cap U$, since $\mcp \cap U$ is closed and analytic in $U$, which gives us that $u\circ F(z) \geq u(v),$ for all $z \in \triangle$. By the maximum principle, $u\circ F$ is constant on $\triangle$, contradicting, again, the strict pseudoconvexity of $S_v$.
nodes.statement_short: Show local transitivity, then rule out the degeneracy divisor $\mcp$ by a Bishop-disk maximum-principle contradiction.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas

nodes.name: Conjugation $\tilde{\sigma}$ on $T^{1,0}G_{\c}$
nodes.statement: Let $T^{1,0}G_{\c}$ be the holomorphic tangent bundle of $G_{\c}$ which is biholomorphic to $G_{\c} \times \mathfrak{g}_{\c},$ an explicit isomorphism given by left-invariant vectorfields on $G_{\c}$. Let $\sigma: G_{\c} \to G_{\c}$ be the complex conjugation such that Fix($\sigma) = G$. Its differential is $D\sigma: T^{1,0}G_{\c} \to T^{0,1}G_{\c}$. This induces a conjugation $\tilde{\sigma}$ on $T^{1,0}G_{\c}$ given by \begin{equation} T^{1,0}G_{\c} \ni \zeta \to \tilde{\sigma}(\zeta) := \overline{D\sigma(\zeta)} \in T^{1,0}G_{\c}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The complex conjugation $\sigma$ fixing $G$ induces a fibrewise conjugation $\tilde\sigma$ on $T^{1,0}G_{\c}$.

nodes.name: Characterization of $\tilde{\sigma}$-real sections
nodes.statement: Then we will identify Fix($\tilde{\sigma}$) = $TG$, and for a section $\zeta$ of $T^{1,0}G_{\c}$ over $G$, we have $\tilde{\sigma}(\zeta) = \zeta$ if and only if $\zeta$ is in the \emph{real} span of $\tilde{\xi}^{1,0}$, with $\xi \in \mfg$ as above, over each $g \in G$. Equivalently, $\zeta(g) \in \{g\} \times \mathfrak{g} \subset G_{\c} \times \mathfrak{g}_{\c}.$
nodes.statement_short: A section is $\tilde\sigma$-fixed exactly when it is real in the left-invariant trivialization.
assumptions: for a section $\zeta$ of $T^{1,0}G_{\c}$ over $G$
conclusions: $\tilde{\sigma}(\zeta) = \zeta$ if and only if $\zeta$ is in the \emph{real} span of $\tilde{\xi}^{1,0}$, with $\xi \in \mfg$ as above, over each $g \in G$

nodes.name: The case $G = \r$ with the Euclidean metric
nodes.statement: To fix ideas, if $G = \r$ (at this point we do not need to assume our group $G$ is compact) with the Euclidean metric and unit tangent vector $\frac{d}{dx}$, so that $\mfg \cong \r \frac{d}{dx} $, then $G_{\c}\cong \c$ with coordinate $z = x+iy$, and $\widetilde{(\frac{d}{dx})}^{1,0} = \frac{\partial}{\partial z}$ on $\c$. In particular, $\frac{\partial}{\partial z}$ is real over $\r = G \subset G_{\c} \cong \c$, and a section $f(z) \frac{\partial}{\partial z}$ of $T^{1,0}G_{\c}$ is $\tilde{\sigma}$-real if and only if $\overline{f(\bar{z})} = f(z)$.
nodes.statement_short: For $G=\r$, $G_{\c}=\c$ and $\tilde\sigma$-reality of $f(z)\partial_z$ means $\overline{f(\bar z)}=f(z)$.

nodes.name: Left-invariant metric $g_A$ from a symmetric positive operator $A$
nodes.statement: A left invariant metric on $M = G$ is given by a symmetric, positive definite transformation $A: \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g}$, where we measure symmetry with respect to the inner product $(\xi, \eta) = - B(\xi, \eta)$, $B$ being the Killing form on $\mathfrak{g}$.
differentia: we measure symmetry with respect to the inner product $(\xi, \eta) = - B(\xi, \eta)$, $B$ being the Killing form on $\mathfrak{g}$

nodes.name: $-B$ gives the round metric of sectional curvature $\frac18$ on $SU(2)$
nodes.statement: If $\mfg$ is simple, the form $-B$ determines the unique (up to constant positive scale) bi-invariant metric on $G$, which is just the round metric of sectional curvature $\frac18$ when $G \cong SU(2) \cong S^3$.
assumptions: If $\mfg$ is simple
conclusions: the form $-B$ determines the unique (up to constant positive scale) bi-invariant metric on $G$, which is just the round metric of sectional curvature $\frac18$ when $G \cong SU(2) \cong S^3$

nodes.name: Unique holomorphic extension of a left-invariant metric to $G_{\c}$
nodes.statement: We extend $A$ to $\mathfrak{g}_{\c}$ by extending scalars, and similarly for $B$ which gives $B_{\c}$, the Killing form for $\mathfrak{g}_{\c}$. This gives a non-degenerate, holomorphic bilinear form on $T^{1,0}G_{\c}$. This form, when restricted to the real sub-bundle $TG \subset T^{1,0}G_{\c}$, induces the original metric on $G$. Otherwise put, every left-invariant metric on $G$ has a unique holomorphic extension to a holomorphic metric on $G_{\c}$.
nodes.statement_short: Every left-invariant metric on $G$ extends uniquely to a holomorphic metric $g_{A,\c}$ on $G_{\c}$.
assumptions: We extend $A$ to $\mathfrak{g}_{\c}$ by extending scalars, and similarly for $B$ which gives $B_{\c}$, the Killing form for $\mathfrak{g}_{\c}$
conclusions: every left-invariant metric on $G$ has a unique holomorphic extension to a holomorphic metric on $G_{\c}$

nodes.name: Normal exponential map $\Phi: TG \to G_{\c}$
nodes.statement: We have a kind of normal exponential map, a smooth mapping $\Phi: TG \to G_{\c}$ given by \begin{equation} \Phi: TG \ni v \to \gamma_{\c}(i v) = Exp_{\c}(i v) \in G_{\c}, \end{equation} where, for $v \neq 0$, $\gamma$ is the real geodesic with $\gamma(0) = \pi(v), \dot{\gamma}(0) = \frac{v}{|v|}$. For $v = 0 \in T_gG, \Phi(v) = g$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Phi$ sends $v \in TG$ to $Exp_{\c}(iv)$, the imaginary-time complex exponential.

nodes.name: Proof that $\Phi$ is globally defined and holomorphic
nodes.statement: This map is, at first, just defined in a neighborhood of the zero section $G$. It is real analytic, $G$-equivariant and sends a real geodesic $\gamma \subset G$ to the real points of the corresponding $g_{\c}$-geodesic. Now if we consider $TG$ with its adapted complex structure, which we will momentarily call $J_T$, and we consider the complex submanifold $T\gamma \subset TM, J_T$, for $\gamma$ a $g$-geodesic, then $\Phi$ restricted to $i T\gamma$ maps it biholomorphically onto a neighborhood of $\gamma \subset \gamma_{\c} \subset G_{\c}$. Since this is true for all geodesics in $G, \Phi$ is holomorphic from $TM, J_T$ to $G_{\c}$. But then $\Phi$ is locally $G_{\c}$-equivariant, and is, locally near the zero section, the inverse of the action map from $G_{\c} \to TM, J_T,$ which is a global biholomorphism, by lemma \ref{lem:homogeneity}. Hence, $\Phi$ is globally defined by analytic extension, and is holomorphic. It embeds every $T\gamma \subset TM, J_T$ onto $\gamma_{\c} \subset G_{\c}$ biholomorphically.
nodes.statement_short: Local biholomorphy along each geodesic plus $G_{\c}$-equivariance and lemma 2.2 extend $\Phi$ analytically to all of $TG$.

nodes.name: Real $g_{\c}$-geodesic
nodes.statement: We call a connected, $\sigma$-invariant complex geodesic curve $\Gamma \subset G_{\c}$ a {\em real} $g_{\c}$-geodesic if $\Gamma$ is the complexification of a real geodesic $\gamma \subset G$.
nodes.genus: a connected, $\sigma$-invariant complex geodesic curve $\Gamma \subset G_{\c}$
differentia: $\Gamma$ is the complexification of a real geodesic $\gamma \subset G$

nodes.name: Real $g_{\c}$-geodesics are complete and foliate $G_{\c}\setminus G$
nodes.statement: Let $g = g_A$ be a left invariant metric on $G$ such that its Grauert tube is entire. Then all real $g_{\c}$-geodesics on $G_{\c}$ for the holomorphic metric $g_{\c} = g_{A, \c}$ are complete. Furthermore, they give a foliation $\mathcal{F}_{\c}$ of $G_{\c} \setminus G$.
nodes.statement_short: An entire tube forces all complexified real geodesics to be complete and to foliate $G_{\c}\setminus G$.
assumptions: Let $g = g_A$ be a left invariant metric on $G$ such that its Grauert tube is entire
conclusions: all real $g_{\c}$-geodesics on $G_{\c}$ for the holomorphic metric $g_{\c} = g_{A, \c}$ are complete
they give a foliation $\mathcal{F}_{\c}$ of $G_{\c} \setminus G$

nodes.name: Differential of $\Phi$ on the group directions
nodes.statement: First, there are the directions in $T_v(TG)$ spanned by the vectors $\tilde{\eta}_x, x \in \mfg$. Since $\Phi$ is $G$-equivariant, \vs \[ D\Phi_{v}(\tilde{\eta}_x)(v) = \eta^{1,0}_{x,\c}(\Phi(v)). \]

nodes.name: Differential of the real exponential map via Jacobi fields
nodes.statement: For the real exponential map $Exp: TG \to G$, we have that \begin{equation} DExp_{t v}(w) = Y_w(\gamma(t)), \end{equation} where $\gamma(t)$ is the (real) geodesic satisfying $\gamma(0) = \pi(v), \dot{\gamma}(0) = v,$ and $Y_w$ is the Jacobi field along $\gamma$ with initial conditions $Y_w(\pi(v)) = 0, \nabla_{\dot{\gamma}}Y_w(\pi(v)) = w.$
nodes.statement_short: $DExp_{tv}(w)$ is the Jacobi field $Y_w$ along $\gamma$ with $Y_w(0)=0$, $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}Y_w(0)=w$.

nodes.name: Holomorphic geodesic equation for $\Gamma$
nodes.statement: Similarly, in the holomorphic geometry of $G_{\c}$,we can consider the holomorphic geodesic $\Gamma(\zeta)$ satisfying \vs \begin{equation} \nabla^{\c}_{\dot{\Gamma}(\zeta)} \dot{\Gamma}(\zeta) = 0, \; \Gamma(0) =\pi(v), \; \dot{\Gamma}(0) = i v \in T^{1,0}_{\pi(v)}(G_{\c}). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Holomorphic analogue of the Jacobi-field differential formula
nodes.statement: and the holomorphic Jacobi field $W^{\c}_w = W^{\c}_w(\Gamma(\zeta)$ along $\Gamma$ satisfying $W_w^{\c}(\pi(v))$ $= 0, \nabla^{\c}_{\dot{\Gamma}} W_w^{\c}(\pi(v)) = w.$ Then we have the holomorphic case of (\ref{eqn:DExp}): \vs\vs \begin{equation} DExp_{\c, i t v }(w) = W^{\c}_w(\Gamma(t)) \in T^{1,0}_{\Gamma(t)}(G_{\c}). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Identities relating $\Gamma$, $W^{\c}_w$ and $D\Phi$
nodes.statement: The following identities hold: \[ \begin{array}{l} \text{(1)}\; \Gamma(\zeta) = \gamma_{\c}(i \zeta) \\ \\ \text{(2)} \; W^{\c}_w(\Gamma(\zeta)) = Y^{\c}(\gamma_{\c}(i \zeta))\\ \\ \text{(3)} \; D\Phi_{t v}(w) = Y^{\c}(\gamma_{\c}(i t v)). \end{array} \]
nodes.statement_short: The holomorphic geodesic and Jacobi field are the imaginary-time rotations of their real counterparts.
conclusions: \text{(1)}\; \Gamma(\zeta) = \gamma_{\c}(i \zeta)
\text{(2)} \; W^{\c}_w(\Gamma(\zeta)) = Y^{\c}(\gamma_{\c}(i \zeta))
\text{(3)} \; D\Phi_{t v}(w) = Y^{\c}(\gamma_{\c}(i t v)).

nodes.name: Proof of the identities for $\Gamma$, $W^{\c}_w$ and $D\Phi$
nodes.statement: (1) and (2) follow from the holomorphy of $\gamma_{\c}, Y^{\c}_w, \Gamma,$ and $W^{\c}_w$, and the uniqueness theorem for holomorphic ODE. (3) is simply (\ref{eqn:DExpC}) taking into account the definition of $\Phi$ (\ref{eqn:Expdef}), and parts (1) and (2).
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness for holomorphic ODEs gives (1) and (2); (3) is then the definition of $\Phi$.

nodes.name: Right-invariant versus left-invariant extension of $X \in \mfg$
nodes.statement: If $X \in \mfg \cong T_eG$, denote by $\eta_X(g) =DR_{g}(X) \in T_gG$ its right-invariant extension over all of $G$, and $\xi_X(g) = DL_{g} X \in T_gG$ its left-invariant extension. Then one has \vs \begin{equation} \eta_X(g) = \xi_{Ad(g^{-1})X}(g) \in T_gG. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\eta_X = \xi_{Ad(g^{-1})X}$ converts right-invariant fields into left-invariant ones.

nodes.name: Jacobi fields expanded in the right-invariant frame
nodes.statement: Let $X_1,\ldots, X_d$ be a real basis of $\mfg$ and let $Y_{X_i}$ be the Jacobi fields as in (\ref{eqn:DExp}) for $w = \eta_{X_i} \in T_{\pi(v)}G.$ Express the $Y_i$ in the basis $\eta_{X-i}$,so that one has \vs \begin{equation} Y^{\c}_i(\gamma_{\c}(\zeta)) = a_{i, 1}(\zeta) \; \eta^{1,0}_{X_1,\c}(\gamma_{\c}(\zeta)) + \ldots + a_{i, d}(\zeta) \; \eta^{1,0}_{X_d, \c}(\gamma_{\c}(\zeta)). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Write the complexified Jacobi fields $Y^{\c}_i$ with coefficient functions $a_{i,j}(\zeta)$ in the frame $\eta^{1,0}_{X_j,\c}$.

nodes.name: Rank formula for $D\Phi_{tv}$
nodes.statement: The rank of $D\Phi_{t v}$ is given by \begin{equation} \text{rank}\; D\Phi_{t v} = d\, + \;{\text{rank}}\; {\; \text{Im} \;} \left(\begin{array}{ccc} a_{1,1}(i t) & \cdots & a_{1,d}(i t) \\ && \\ & \cdots & \\ && \\ a_{d, 1}(i t) & \cdots & a_{d,d}(i t) \end{array} \right), \end{equation} where the rank of $D\Phi_{t v}$ means the real rank of the differential, and $Im$ is the imaginary part.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{rank}\, D\Phi_{tv} = d + \mathrm{rank}\,\mathrm{Im}\,(a_{i,j}(it))$.
conclusions: where the rank of $D\Phi_{t v}$ means the real rank of the differential, and $Im$ is the imaginary part

nodes.name: Energy $E$ and total angular momentum $M$
nodes.statement: At this point we specialize to the case $G = SU(2)$, which has two explicit mechanical integrals. Notation as above, at the beginning of section \ref{sec:Gcgeom}, these are the energy $E = (Av,v),$ and the total angular momentum $M = (A^2v,v)$.
nodes.statement_short: The two mechanical first integrals of the $SU(2)$ rigid body: $E=(Av,v)$ and $M=(A^2v,v)$.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals
nodes.definiendum: the energy $E$ and the total angular momentum $M$

nodes.name: Complete integrability of the geodesic system on $SU(2)$
nodes.statement: Taken together with any Hamiltonian generating a one-parameter group in $G$ acting on the tangent bundle shows that the geodesic system, with Hamiltonian $E$, is completely integrable.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals
assumptions: Taken together with any Hamiltonian generating a one-parameter group in $G$ acting on the tangent bundle
conclusions: the geodesic system, with Hamiltonian $E$, is completely integrable

nodes.name: The quadratic integrals are constant along complexified geodesics
nodes.statement: If we write the complex geodesic in $T^{1,0}G_{\c}$ as $\tilde{\gamma}(\zeta) = (\gamma(\zeta), v(\zeta)) \in G_{\c} \times \mfg_{\c},$ with $\zeta \in \c$, the quadratic integrals are functions of $v(\zeta)$ alone, so that $E(v(\zeta)), M(v(\zeta))$ are constant along $\tilde{\gamma}$. If the complex geodesic is real, then the values $E(v(\zeta_0)) = a, M(v(\zeta_0)) = b$, are real and positive.
nodes.statement_short: $E(v(\zeta))$ and $M(v(\zeta))$ are constant along a complex geodesic, and real positive when it is real.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals
assumptions: If we write the complex geodesic in $T^{1,0}G_{\c}$ as $\tilde{\gamma}(\zeta) = (\gamma(\zeta), v(\zeta)) \in G_{\c} \times \mfg_{\c},$ with $\zeta \in \c$
conclusions: the quadratic integrals are functions of $v(\zeta)$ alone, so that $E(v(\zeta)), M(v(\zeta))$ are constant along $\tilde{\gamma}$
the values $E(v(\zeta_0)) = a, M(v(\zeta_0)) = b$, are real and positive

nodes.name: Projective quadrics $\q_{E,a}$ and $\q_{M,b}$
nodes.statement: In homogeneous coordinates $z_1, z_2, z_3, w$, the quadrics $\q_{E,a}, \q_{M,b}$ are given by \vs \begin{equation} 0 = \lambda_1 \, z_1^2 + \lambda_2 \, z_2^2 + \lambda_3 \, z_3^2 - a \, w^2, \end{equation} \begin{equation} 0 = \lambda_1^2 \, z_1^2 + \lambda_2^2 \, z_2^2 + \lambda_3^2 \, z_3^2 - b \, w^2, \end{equation}\vs {\em respectively}.
nodes.statement_short: The level sets of energy and angular momentum are two projective quadrics in $\p^3$.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: $A$ diagonalized with positive eigenvalues
nodes.statement: Here we have assumed, without loss of generality, that $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3 \in \r^+$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and that $A$ has been diagonalized. One should observe that this can be done by the adjoint action of $SU(2)$ on its Lie algebra.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: The curve $C_{a,b}$
nodes.statement: If $[\lambda_1: \lambda_2: \lambda_3: a] \neq [\lambda_1^2: \lambda_2^2: \lambda_3^2: b]$, then the intersection of these two quadrics is a curve in $\p^3$ which we denote by $C_{a,b}$.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals
differentia: the intersection of these two quadrics

nodes.name: Independence of the parameters $a$ and $b$
nodes.statement: The set of real parameters $(x_1, x_2, x_3) \in \r^3$ such that $a = E(x)$ and $b = M(x)$ verify \begin{equation} b \neq \lambda_k \; a, \; k = 1, 2, 3, \end{equation} has non-empty interior.
nodes.statement_short: The parameters with $b \neq \lambda_k a$ for all $k$ form a set with non-empty interior.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals
assumptions: The set of real parameters $(x_1, x_2, x_3) \in \r^3$ such that $a = E(x)$ and $b = M(x)$ verify
conclusions: b \neq \lambda_k \; a, \; k = 1, 2, 3,
has non-empty interior

nodes.name: Proof that generic $(a,b)$ form a set with non-empty interior
nodes.statement: It suffices to consider the map \[ F(x) := \left(\begin{array}{c} E(x) \\ \\ M(x) \end{array}\right) \] and show the differential is surjective for some $x \in \r^3$. But this differential is \[ DF(x) = \left(\begin{array}{ccc} 2\lambda_1 \, x_1 & 2\lambda_2 \, x_2 & 2\lambda_3 x_3 \\ & & \\ 2\lambda_1^2 \, x_1 & 2\lambda_2^2 \, x_2 & 2\lambda_3^2 \, x_3 \end{array} \right), \] whose minor determinants are (up to a factor of $\pm2$) \[ \begin{array}{l} \lambda_1 \, \lambda_2 \, (\lambda_2 - \lambda_1) \, x_1 \, x_2,\\ \\ \lambda_1 \, \lambda_3 \, (\lambda_3 - \lambda_1) \, x_1 \, x_3, \; \text{and}\\ \\ \lambda_2 \, \lambda_3 \, (\lambda_3 - \lambda_2) \, x_2 \, x_3. \end{array} \] Since we are assuming that not all $\lambda_i$ are equal, then choosing all $x_i$ non-zero will give maximal rank.
nodes.statement_short: Show $DF$ has maximal rank by computing the $2\times2$ minors of $(E,M)$.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Generic parameters $a, b$
nodes.statement: We will call $a, b$ {\em generic} if $a, b$ satisfy the conclusion of the lemma.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: $C_{a,b}$ is smooth of genus 1 for pairwise distinct $\lambda_i$
nodes.statement: Suppose the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of $A$ are pairwise distinct, and $a, b$ are generic, as in lemma \ref{lem:gpab}. Then the projective curve $C_{a,b}$ is smooth, of genus 1.
nodes.statement_short: For distinct eigenvalues and generic $(a,b)$ the intersection curve is a smooth elliptic curve.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals
assumptions: Suppose the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of $A$ are pairwise distinct, and $a, b$ are generic, as in lemma \ref{lem:gpab}
conclusions: the projective curve $C_{a,b}$ is smooth, of genus 1

nodes.name: Classical genus formula
nodes.statement: To complete the proof, we use the classical genus formula \[ g(C_{a,b}) = 1 + \frac12 \; C_{a,b} \cdot (C_{a,b} + K_{\q_{E,a}}), \] where $K_{\q_{E,a}}$ is the canonical class of $\q_{E,a} \sim -2 H$, where $H$ in turn is the hyperplane section of $\q_{E,a} \subset \p^3$.
nodes.statement_short: Adjunction on the quadric $\q_{E,a}$ computes the genus of $C_{a,b}$.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Proof that $C_{a,b}$ is smooth of genus 1
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be the two by four matrix \[ B = \left(\begin{array}{cccc} \lambda_1 z_1 & \lambda_2 \, z_2 & \lambda_3 \, z_3 & - a \, w \\ & & & \\ \lambda_1^2 \, z_1 & \lambda_2^2 \, z_2 & \lambda_3^2 \, z_3 & - b \, w \end{array} \right). \] We wish to show that there are no $(z_1, z_2, z_3, w) \neq (0,0,0,0)$ which solve (\ref{eqn:qe}) and (\ref{eqn:qm}), and for which the rank of $B$ is $<$ 2, or the six $2\times 2$ minors of $B$ are 0: \[ \begin{array}{rcl} 0 & = & \lambda_1 \, \lambda_2 (\lambda_2 - \lambda_1) \, z_1 \, z_2 \\ \\ 0 & = & \lambda_1 \, \lambda_3 \,(\lambda_3 - \lambda_1)\, z_1\, z_3 \\ \\ 0 & = & \lambda_2 \, \lambda_3 \, (\lambda_3 - \lambda_2)\, z_2 \, z_3 \\ \\ 0 & = & \lambda_1\, (b - \lambda_1 \, a) \, z_1 \, w\\ \\ 0 & = & \lambda_2 \, (b - \lambda_2 \, a) \, z_2 \, w \\ \\ 0 & = & \lambda_3 \, (b - \lambda_3 \, a) \, z_3 \, w. \end{array} \] On the other hand, it is clear that any 4-tuple $(z_1, z_2, z_3, w)$ satisfying (\ref{eqn:qe}) or (\ref{eqn:qm}) must have at least two non-zero components, while on the other hand, all the constants in this last array of equations are non-zero under our assumptions. This is a contradiction, hence $C_{a,b}$ is smooth. \vs To complete the proof, we use the classical genus formula \[ g(C_{a,b}) = 1 + \frac12 \; C_{a,b} \cdot (C_{a,b} + K_{\q_{E,a}}), \] where $K_{\q_{E,a}}$ is the canonical class of $\q_{E,a} \sim -2 H$, where $H$ in turn is the hyperplane section of $\q_{E,a} \subset \p^3$. Since $C_{a,b} \sim 2 H$, we see that $g(C) = 1$, as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Rule out rank-deficient points of the Jacobian $B$ by contradiction, then apply the adjunction genus formula.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Proof that generic left-invariant metrics have non-entire complexified geodesics
nodes.statement: Now the map $v: \c \to C_{a,b} \subset \p^3$ associated to a complexified geodesic with initial conditions $a = E(\gamma(0)), b = M(\gamma(0)),$ must actually map into the affine piece $C^{{aff}}_{a,b} = C_{a,b} \cap \mfg_{\c} = C_{a,b} \setminus C_{a,b} \cap \{w = 0\}$. But this last intersection is non-empty and a holomorphic map of $\c$ to $C^{aff}_{a,b}$ must factor through the universal covering $\pi: \mathbb{C} \to C_{a,b}$, but must omit the infinite set $\pi^{-1}(C_{a,b} \cap\{w = 0\})$. Thus, the map $c$ must be constant, by Picard's theorem. In real terms, this means that the real geodesic satisfies \[ \dot{\gamma} \equiv \xi \in \mfg, \] If we assume, without loss of generality, that $\gamma(0) = e \in G,$ this means that $\gamma(s)$ is the 1-parameter subgroup $\exp(s \xi)$ of $G$. Now this conclusion holds true for all initial conditions $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_0$ in a dense open set of $\mfg = T_0G.$ By continuity of solution of ODEs, this must hold true for all geodesics passing through 0, and hence, by left translation, for all geodesics. However, it is well-known that any left invariant metric for which all geodesics through $e$ are 1-parameter subgroups is necessarily bi-invariant and hence round (see e.g. \cite{o}, ch. 11, Proposition 9). This would contradict our assumption that the $\lambda_i$ are all distinct.
nodes.statement_short: Picard's theorem forces $v$ constant, making all geodesics 1-parameter subgroups, hence the metric bi-invariant - a contradiction.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Metrics whose geodesics through $e$ are 1-parameter subgroups are bi-invariant
nodes.statement: However, it is well-known that any left invariant metric for which all geodesics through $e$ are 1-parameter subgroups is necessarily bi-invariant and hence round (see e.g. \cite{o}, ch. 11, Proposition 9).
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals
assumptions: any left invariant metric for which all geodesics through $e$ are 1-parameter subgroups
conclusions: is necessarily bi-invariant and hence round

nodes.name: Elementary alternative proof via the geodesic equations
nodes.statement: {\em Remark:} One can give a more elementary proof of this last statement using (\ref{eqn:geodeqns}) in the appendix \cite{web} to show that, if the $\lambda$'s are distinct, $\gamma(t)$ is a geodesic with $\gamma(0) = e \in G$, then $T = \dot{\gamma}$ is constant in the left invariant frame if and only if $\gamma(t)$ is a geodesic $\exp(t \, \nu \, \xi_i), i = 1, 2,$ or $3$, for some real constant $\nu$.
nodes.statement_short: The same conclusion follows elementarily from the appendix geodesic equations.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Two equal eigenvalues correspond to isometry group $G \times S^1$
nodes.statement: Next, consider the case where two of the $\lambda_i$ are equal. This is equivalent to the fact that the identity component of the isometry group of $g_A$ is $G\times S^1$ where the extra circle group is a 1-parameter subgroup of $G$ operating on the right.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals
assumptions: the case where two of the $\lambda_i$ are equal
conclusions: the identity component of the isometry group of $g_A$ is $G\times S^1$ where the extra circle group is a 1-parameter subgroup of $G$ operating on the right

nodes.name: Reduction of the quadric pair when $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$
nodes.statement: To be specific, we set $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$, the other case being similar. In this case, equations (\ref{eqn:qe}) and (\ref{eqn:qm}) can be reduced to the pair of equations (\ref{eqn:qe}) and \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcl} 0 & = & (\lambda_1 \lambda_3 - \lambda_3^2) \, z_3^2 - (\lambda_1 \, a - b) \, w^2 \\ & & \\ & = & \lambda_3 \, (\lambda_1 - \lambda_3) \, ( z_3^2 - \frac{\lambda_1 \, a - b}{\lambda_3 \, (\lambda_1 - \lambda_3)} \, w^2) \end{array} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: When $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$ the two quadrics reduce to a factorizable equation in $z_3, w$.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: $C_{a,b}$ splits into two conics biholomorphic to $\c^*$
nodes.statement: It follows that (\ref{eqn:split}) splits over $\r$ and the curve defined by (\ref{eqn:qe}) and (\ref{eqn:split}) is the union of two curves \[ C^+_{a,b} = \q_{E,a} \cap \{ z_3 = x_3^o \, w\} \] and \[ C^-_{a,b} = \q_{E,a} \cap \{z_3 = - x_3^o \, w\}. \] Each of these curves is a conic $\p^1 \subset \p^3$ which intersects the plane at infinity $\{w = 0\}$ in two points generically, so $C^{\text{aff}, \pm}_{a,b}$ is generically biholomorphic to $\c^*$, which certainly contains the images of non-trivial entire mappings from $\c$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$ the curve splits into two conics whose affine parts are $\c^*$, which do admit entire maps.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals
assumptions: It follows that (\ref{eqn:split}) splits over $\r$
conclusions: the curve defined by (\ref{eqn:qe}) and (\ref{eqn:split}) is the union of two curves
$C^{\text{aff}, \pm}_{a,b}$ is generically biholomorphic to $\c^*$, which certainly contains the images of non-trivial entire mappings from $\c$

nodes.name: The distinct-eigenvalue method fails when $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$
nodes.statement: Thus the method of proof for the case of $\lambda_i$ pairwise distinct will not work here. In fact, if $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$ then the tube of the metric $g_A$ is sometimes entire.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Normal form of the $U(2)$-symmetric left-invariant metric
nodes.statement: By scaling and renumbering, we can reduce to the case \begin{equation} g_A(v,v) = v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \lambda v_3^2, \end{equation} where $\lambda > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: After scaling, the $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$ metrics are $v_1^2+v_2^2+\lambda v_3^2$ with $\lambda>0$.

nodes.name: Grauert tube of $g_A$ is entire for $\lambda \leq 1$
nodes.statement: Let $g_A$ be as in (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) with $\lambda \leq 1$. Then the Grauert tube of $g_A$ is entire.
assumptions: Let $g_A$ be as in (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) with $\lambda \leq 1$
conclusions: Then the Grauert tube of $g_A$ is entire

nodes.name: Product metric $g_{\mu}$ on $G \times S^1$
nodes.statement: Consider the manifold $G \times S^1$, where $G$ is given the bi-invariant metric of sectional curvature 1, which is the special case of (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) with $\lambda_1= 1$, and the $S^1$ factor is given the metric $\mu d\theta^2,$ where $d\theta^2$ is the invariant metric of length $2\pi$ on $S^1$ and $\mu$ is a real constant $> 0$. So $G\times S^1$ has the metric $g_{\mu}$ defined by \begin{equation} g_{\mu} = g_I \oplus \mu \, d\theta^2. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Equip $G\times S^1$ with the round metric on $G$ plus $\mu\,d\theta^2$ on the circle.

nodes.name: The diagonal matrix $A = \mathrm{diag}(1,1,\lambda)$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} A = \left(\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & & \\ & 1 & \\ & & \lambda \end{array}\right). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Normalization of the metric $g_A$ on the basis $\xi_i$
nodes.statement: Explicitly, we will normalize our metrics so that $g_A(\xi_1, \xi_1) = g_A(\xi_2, \xi_2) = \frac14,$ and $g_A(\xi_3, \xi_3) = \frac{\lambda}4$.

nodes.name: Proof that the tube is entire for $\lambda \leq 1$
nodes.statement: This is an immediate consequence of a result of Sz\H{o}ke \cite{s2} (cf also \cite{a1}). The metric (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) has an isometry group $G \times S^1$ where the factor $S^1$ acts by right multiplication on $G$ by the 1-parameter subgroup $e^{t\, \xi_3}$ on the right, i.e., by $R_{e^{t\, \xi_3}}$, periodic of period $2\pi$, and the factor $G$ acts by left multiplication $L_g$ on $G$. Consider the manifold $G \times S^1$, where $G$ is given the bi-invariant metric of sectional curvature 1, which is the special case of (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) with $\lambda_1= 1$, and the $S^1$ factor is given the metric $\mu d\theta^2,$ where $d\theta^2$ is the invariant metric of length $2\pi$ on $S^1$ and $\mu$ is a real constant $> 0$. So $G\times S^1$ has the metric $g_{\mu}$ defined by \begin{equation} g_{\mu} = g_I \oplus \mu \, d\theta^2. \end{equation} Consider the quotient manifold of $G\times S^1$ by the action of $S^1 = \{e^{i t}\}$ on $G\times S^1$ given by $e^{i t} \cdot (g, e^{i \theta}) = (g\cdot e^{2 t\, \xi_3}, e^{i(\theta + t)}).$ Then it is easy to see that the quotient manifold $G\times S^1/\sim$ is diffeomorphic to $G$. Let $\bar{g}_{\mu}$ be the Riemannian submersion metric from (\ref{eqn:gmu}). By construction, this metric is invariant under left translation by $G$ and by right translation by $e^{- t \, \xi_3}$. Consequently, it is one of the left invariant metrics on $G$ with an extra isometric action from the right. It is an easy calculation to see which ones arise in this manner. Let \begin{equation} A = \left(\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & & \\ & 1 & \\ & & \lambda \end{array}\right). \end{equation} Explicitly, we will normalize our metrics so that $g_A(\xi_1, \xi_1) = g_A(\xi_2, \xi_2) = \frac14,$ and $g_A(\xi_3, \xi_3) = \frac{\lambda}4$.\footnote{This means that instead of $g_A(\cdot,\cdot) = -B(A(\cdot), \cdot)$, we now have $g_A(\cdot, \cdot) = -\frac18 B(A(\cdot), \cdot)$.} With this normalization, the case $A = I$ gives the round metric with sectional curvature $K = 1$ on $G \cong S^3$. \vs We want to see which $\lambda$ in (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) will arise from Sz\H{o}ke's construction. Computing at $(e,1) \in G\times S^1$, the tangent vector to the $S^1$ action we will quotient by is given by $(2\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta})$. The projection of $(\xi_3, 0)$ onto this direction is given by \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcl} (\xi_3,0)^T & = & \frac{((\xi_3, 0), (\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}))}{|\xi_3 + \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}|^2} (\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}), \\ & & \\ & = & \frac2{2+\mu} (\xi_3, \dbdth) \end{array} \end{equation} and hence the normal component is given by \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcl} (\xi_3,0)^N & = & (\xi_3,0) - (\xi_3,0)^T \\ & & \\ & = & (\frac{\mu}{2+\mu} \xi_3, \frac2{2+\mu} \dbdth). \end{array} \end{equation} Thus, \[ |\xi_3^N|^2 = 2 \frac{\mu}{2+\mu}, \] which means that the quotient metric on $G$ is $g_A$ with $A$ in (\ref{eqn:A}) having $\lambda = \frac{\mu}{2 + \mu}.$ Hence, any $\lambda \in (0, 1)$ appears. The limit case $\mu = +\infty$ is just the case of the round sphere, $\lambda = 1$, which also has an entire tube, of course.
nodes.statement_short: Realize $g_A$ as a Riemannian submersion quotient of $G\times S^1$ and invoke Sz\H{o}ke's homogeneous-quotient theorem.

nodes.name: Metrics with $\lambda > 1$ have tubes of finite radius
nodes.statement: Finally, there remains the case of (\ref{eqn:A}) with $\lambda > 1$. These metrics have tubes of finite radius, and we study the complexified Jacobi equation to determine this radius. We first observe that, in contrast to the case of a generic $A$, the map $Exp_{g_{A,\c}}$ is globally defined for real initial conditions, i.e., on $TG$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\lambda>1$ the tube has finite radius, though $Exp_{g_{A,\c}}$ is still globally defined on $TG$.
assumptions: the case of (\ref{eqn:A}) with $\lambda > 1$
conclusions: These metrics have tubes of finite radius

nodes.name: $g_{A,\c}$ exponential map is defined and smooth on all of $TG$
nodes.statement: For a metric $g_A$ with $G\times S^1$ symmetry (\ref{eqn:A}), the $g_{A,\c}$ exponential map is defined and smooth on all of $TG$.
assumptions: For a metric $g_A$ with $G\times S^1$ symmetry (\ref{eqn:A})
conclusions: the $g_{A,\c}$ exponential map is defined and smooth on all of $TG$

nodes.name: Proof that $Exp_{g_{A,\c}}$ is globally defined on $TG$
nodes.statement:
Let $\gamma$ be the real geodesic on $G$ with initial conditions $\gamma(0) = e \in G$ and $\dot{\gamma}(0) = v_0 \in T_eG \cong \mfg$. We solve the geodesic equations (ef{eqn:geodeqns1}) in the appendix \cite{web} relatively explicitly to show that the complexified geodesic $\gamma_{\c}(\zeta)$ is an entire function from $\c$ to $G_{\c}$. The other statements in the proposition follow from smooth dependence on initial conditions. \vs For convenience, we repeat here the equations (ef{eqn:geodeqns1}) from \cite{web} for the tangent vector $T = a\, \xi_1+b\, \xi_2+c\, \xi_3$ to a geodesic, subject to the initial condition $T(0) = a_0 \, \xi_1+ b_0\, \xi_2 +c_0 \, \xi_3,$ for a metric of the form $g_A$, with $A$ as in (ef{eqn:A}): \[  egin{array}{rcl} \dot{a} & = & -b\, c\, (\lambda - 1) \ &&\ \dot{b} & = & - a\, c\, (1 - \lambda) \ &&\ \dot{c} & = & 0, \end{array} \] where $\dot{a} = T(a)$, etc. We get that $c \equiv c_0 \in $, and the system reduces to \[  egin{array}{rcr} \dot{a} & = & -
u\, b \ &&\ \dot{b} & = & 
u \, a, \end{array} \] with $
u = c_0 \, (\lambda - 1) \in $. Hence, \vs \[  egin{array}{rcl} a & \equiv & a_0 \cos 
u \, t - b_0 \sin 
u \,t \&&\ b & \equiv & b_0 \cos 
u \,t + a_0 \sin 
u \, t, \end{array} \] \vs where $t$ is the parameter of integration in the equations. Set \[ T_{\c} = a(\zeta) \, \xi_{1,\c} +b(\zeta) \, \xi_{2,\c} + c_0 \, \xi_{3,\c}, \] which is an entire function from $\c 	o \mathfrak{sl}(2,\c) \subset \c^4.$ Considering $\gamma_{\c}$ as a function from, at first, a neighborhood of $ \subset \c$ to $G_{\c} = SL(2,\c) \subset \c^4$, we have that it satisfies the equation \[ \gamma_{\c}(\zeta)^{-1} \cdot \dot{\gamma_{\c}} = T_{\c}, \] where $\dot{\gamma}_{\c} =  rac{d\;\;}{d \zeta}$, since we are using the left-invariant parallelism to trivialize $T^{1,0}G_{\c}$. Equivalently, we have \[ \dot{\gamma}_{\c} = \gamma_{\c} \cdot T_{\c}, \] which is a linear equation, with $T_{\c}$ entire and known, on all of $\c$. Hence all its solutions extend to entire functions, proving the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the reduced geodesic ODE explicitly, so $T_{\c}$ is entire and $\dot\gamma_{\c}=\gamma_{\c}T_{\c}$ is a linear ODE with entire solutions.

nodes.name: $\Phi$ is defined and smooth on all of $TG$; singularity for $\lambda>1$
nodes.statement: Because of lemma \ref{lem:Expdefd}, the map $\Phi$ of section \ref{sec:Gcgeom} is defined and smooth on all of $TG$. We next show that for $\lambda> 1$ this map has a singularity at $t_*(\lambda) \in \r_+.$

nodes.name: $D\Phi$ is singular at $(e, t_*(\lambda)\xi_1)$ for $\lambda > 1$
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be as in (\ref{eqn:A}) with $\lambda> 1$. Then $D\Phi$ is singular at $(e, t_*(\lambda) \xi_1) \in T_eG \cong \mfg,$ for some $t_*(\lambda) \in (0,\infty)$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\lambda>1$ a focal point occurs at finite time $t_*(\lambda)$, bounding the tube radius.
assumptions: Let $A$ be as in (\ref{eqn:A}) with $\lambda> 1$
conclusions: $D\Phi$ is singular at $(e, t_*(\lambda) \xi_1) \in T_eG \cong \mfg,$ for some $t_*(\lambda) \in (0,\infty)$

nodes.name: Proof of the existence of a focal point for $\lambda > 1$
nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lem:rankDPhi}, to find singularities of $D\Phi$ at points $t v \in T_eG$, it suffices to \vs \begin{enumerate} \item Solve the Jacobi equation $\mathcal{J}_1(Y) = 0, Y = f \,\xi_2 + h\, \xi_3,$ along $\gamma$, the geodesic in $G$ with initial condition $\gamma(0) = e \in G$, and $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_1 \in T_eG \cong \mfg$.\vs\vs \item Set $Y_i = f_i\, \xi_2 + h_i \, \xi_3, i =2, 3,$ where $f_i(0) = h_i(0) = 0,$ and \vs \begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2'(0)& h_2'(0) \\& \\f_3'(0) & h_3'(0) \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 0 \\& \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right). \end{equation}\vs\vs \item Express $Y_{i,\c} = \alpha_i\, \eta_{2,\c}^{1,0} + \beta_i \, \eta_{3,\c}^{1,0}, i = 2,3.$\vs\vs \item Evaluate \[\Delta(t) = \det Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \beta_2(i t) \\ & \\ \alpha_3(i t) & \beta_3(i t) \end{array} \right).\] Solve $\Delta(t) = 0$. \end{enumerate}\vs\vs We will show that $\Delta(t) = 0$ has a unique root $t_*(\lambda) \in (0, +\infty)$, proving the proposition. \vs\vs Step (1) is calculated in section \ref{sub:JacA}, (\ref{eqn:Jac1soln}): \[ \begin{array}{rcl} f & = & a \cos t + b \sin t + c\\&&\\h & = & b \cos t - a \sin t + \frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda} c t + d, \end{array} \] where $a, b, c ,d \in \r$. (2) says, first, that $c = - a, d = - b,$ and further the first order initial conditions say \vs \[ \begin{array}{rcccl} f'_2(0) & = & b & =& 1 \\&&&&\\h'_2(0) & =& - \frac{a}{\lambda} & = & 0\end{array} \] \vs and \vs \[ \begin{array}{rcccl}f'_3(0) & = & b & = & 0\\ &&&&\\ h'_3(0) & = & - \frac{a}{\lambda} & =& 1.\end{array} \] \vs Hence, in the basis $\xi_2, \xi_3$ for normal fields to $\gamma$, we have \vs \begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2 & f_3 \\&\\ h_2 & h_3 \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\ \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right). \end{equation} \vs As to step (3), as in $(\ref{eqn:xi2eta})$ we have at $g \in \exp t \xi_1$ the change of basis from the $\xi$'s to the $\eta$'s is given by the action $Ad(- t \xi_1)$, explicitly: \vs \[ \begin{array}{rcccl} \eta_2 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \, \xi_2 & = & \cos t \; \xi_2 + \sin t \; \xi_3, \\ &&&&\\ \eta_3 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \xi_3 & = & - \sin t \; \xi_2 + \cos t \; \xi_3. \end{array} \] \vs so that we have \vs \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2 & \alpha_3\\ & \\ \beta_2 & \beta_3 \end{array}\right) & = & \left( \begin{array}{cc} \cos t & - \sin t \\& \\ \sin t & \cos t \end{array}\right) \cdot \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\ \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right) \\ && \\ & = & \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & \lambda [(\cos t - 1) + \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \sin t] \\ & \\ - (\cos t -1) & \lambda [\sin t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cos t] \end{array}\right). \end{array} \] \vs It follows directly that \vs \[ Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \alpha_3(i t) \\ & \\ \beta_2(i t) & \beta_3(i t)\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sinh t & 0 \\ & \\ 0 & \lambda [\sinh t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cosh t] \end{array}\right). \] \vs Finally, we have $\Delta(t) = 0$ if and only if \vs \begin{equation} \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t = \tanh t. \end{equation} \vs It is clear pictorially or from an elementary calculus computation that, if $\lambda >1$, there is a unique $t_*(\lambda) > 0$ satisfying (\ref{eqn:tstar}), as claimed
nodes.statement_short: Solve the Jacobi system, change to the right-invariant frame, and show $\det\mathrm{Im}$ vanishes exactly when $\frac{\lambda-1}{\lambda}t=\tanh t$.

nodes.name: Focal-time equation $\frac{\lambda-1}{\lambda}t = \tanh t$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t = \tanh t. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Extend the study to groups other than $SU(2)$
nodes.statement: Can one carry out such a study as here for groups other than $SU(2)$? It would seem to require integrability with especially simple integrals, such as the quadratic polynomials here.

nodes.name: Determine the finite tube radius for $\lambda \in (1,+\infty)$
nodes.statement: It may also be possible to determine the finite radius of the tubes for $\lambda \in (1,+\infty)$ using the explicit solution for the tangent vector along a geodesic for such geometries, as in section \ref{sec:U2cases} above.

nodes.name: Tube-radius estimate via Ahlfors-Schwarz-Pick
nodes.statement: One might also find an estimate for the tube radius using an approximation to the constant negative curvature metrics on the affine elliptic curves given by the complex integrals of motion and the Ahlfors-Schwarz-Pick inequality. It is unclear how such bounds would compare to the Lempert-Sz\H{o}ke curvature bound when both bounds apply.

nodes.name: Non-normal compact Riemannian homogeneous spaces $G/H$
nodes.statement: Finally, can anything interesting be said of the case of a compact Riemannian homogeneous space $G/H$ which is not normal, i.e., not the Riemannian quotient of a symmetric metric on $G$?

nodes.name: Gelfand-Cetlin quantum integrable systems on flag manifolds
nodes.statement: A related question would be whether Gelfand-Cetlin quantum integrable systems exist on flag manifolds, which contain the Laplacian for a non-normal homogeneous metric.

nodes.name: Structure constants of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$
nodes.statement: The case of $\mfg = \mathfrak{su}(2)$ is particularly simple in this regard, since we can find an orthonormal basis for $(\cdot,\cdot)$ consisting of $\xi_i, i = 1,2,3,$ with brackets given by \begin{equation} [\xi_i, \xi_{i+1}] = \xi_{i+2}, \end{equation} where the indices are read$\mod 3$, i.e., permuted cyclically.
nodes.statement_short: An orthonormal basis $\xi_i$ of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with $[\xi_i,\xi_{i+1}]=\xi_{i+2}$ cyclically.
nodes.section: 7.1 The Levi-Civita connection of $g_A$ on $G = SU(2)$

nodes.name: The basis $\xi_i$ also diagonalizes $A$
nodes.statement: In fact, if we are given $A$ as above, we can assume this basis also diagonalizes $A$ on $\mfg$: \begin{equation} A(\xi_i) = \lambda_i \, \xi_i, i = 1,2,3, \,\text{with} \, 0 < \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \lambda_3, \end{equation}
nodes.section: 7.1 The Levi-Civita connection of $g_A$ on $G = SU(2)$

nodes.name: Standard formula for the Levi-Civita connection
nodes.statement:
Let us first recall the standard formula for the Levi-Civita connection for an arbitrary Riemannian manifold, where momentarily, $(\cdot,\cdot)=g$ is arbitrary and $
abla$ its Levi-Civita connection. Let $X, Y, Z$ be arbitrary smooth vectorfields, then $
abla$ is determined by:  egin{equation}  egin{array}{rcl} (
abla_X\, Y, Z) & = &  rac12 \{X(Y, Z) - Z(X, Y) + Y(Z, X) +\ & & \ & & (Z, [X, Y]) + ([Z, X], Y) + (X, [Z, Y]) \}. \end{array} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The Koszul formula determining $\nabla$ from the metric and brackets.
nodes.section: 7.1 The Levi-Civita connection of $g_A$ on $G = SU(2)$

nodes.name: Levi-Civita connection for a left-invariant metric
nodes.statement: Specializing now to our case of a left-invariant metric on $G$, we get \begin{equation} (\naba_{\xi}\, \eta, \zeta)_A = \frac12\{ (\zeta, [\xi, \eta])_A + ([\zeta, \xi], \eta)_A + (\xi, [\zeta, \eta])_A\}, \end{equation} where $\xi, \eta, \zeta$ are left-invariant fields in $\mfg$.
nodes.statement_short: The Koszul formula reduces to a purely algebraic bracket identity on $\mfg$.
nodes.section: 7.1 The Levi-Civita connection of $g_A$ on $G = SU(2)$

nodes.name: Explicit covariant derivatives $\nabla^A_{\xi_j}\xi_i$ on $SU(2)$
nodes.statement:
In particular, if $G = SU(2)$, we can use the basis $\xi_1, \xi_2, \xi_3$ from (ef{eqn:structureconstants}) and (ef{eqn:eigenbasis}) to get explicitly:  egin{equation} 
aba_{\xi_j}\, \xi_i = \sum_k a_{i; j}^k \xi_k, \end{equation} where the $a_{i; j}^k$ are real constants given by  egin{equation}  egin{array}{rcl} 0 & = & 
aba_{\xi^1}\xi_1 = 
aba_{\xi_2}\xi_2 = 
aba_{\xi_3}\xi_3 , \end{array} \end{equation} and  egin{equation}  egin{array}{rcl} 
aba_{\xi_1}\xi_2 & = &  rac1{2\lambda_3}\{-\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3\} \, \xi_3 \ & & \ 
aba_{\xi_1}\xi_3 & = &  rac1{2 \lambda_2} \{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2 - \lambda_3\}\, \xi_2 \ & & \ 
aba_{\xi_2} \xi_1 & = & \,  rac1{2 \lambda_3} \{-\lambda_1 +\lambda_2 - \lambda_3\} \, \xi_3 \ & & \ 
aba_{\xi_2} \xi_3 & = &  rac1{2 \lambda_1} \{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2 + \lambda_3\} \, \xi_1\ & & \ 
aba_{\xi_3} \xi_1 & = &  rac1{2 \lambda_2}\{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 - \lambda_3\} \, \xi_2 \ & & \ 
aba_{\xi_3} \xi_2 & = & \,  rac1{2 \lambda_1} \{-\lambda_1 - \lambda_2 + \lambda_3\} \, \xi_1 \end{array} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: All six mixed covariant derivatives of the eigenbasis, with the diagonal ones vanishing.
