nodes.name: Geodesic equations for $g_A$ on $SU(2)$
nodes.statement: Use (\ref{eqn:1pggeod}) and (\ref{eqn:covder}) to reduce these to \begin{equation} \begin{array}{lcr} \dot{a} & = & - \frac{bc}{\lambda_1}(\lambda_3 - \lambda_2),\\ &&\\ \dot{b} & = & - \frac{ac}{\lambda_2}(\lambda_1 - \lambda_3),\\ &&\\ \dot{c} & = & - \frac{ab}{\lambda_3}(\lambda_2 - \lambda_1). \end{array} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The Euler equations $\dot a = -\frac{bc}{\lambda_1}(\lambda_3-\lambda_2)$ etc. for the geodesic tangent.

nodes.name: Geodesic equations when $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = 1$
nodes.statement: A special case of interest is when $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = 1, \lambda_3 := \lambda,$ where the equations reduce to \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcl} \dot{a} & = & -bc(\lambda - 1) \\ &&\\ \dot{b} & = & - ac(1 - \lambda) \\ &&\\ \dot{c} & = & 0. \end{array} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: In the $U(2)$-symmetric case the third component $c$ is constant and $(a,b)$ rotate.

nodes.name: Eigenspaces of the curvature operator under the extra $S^1$ symmetry
nodes.statement: We view the Riemann curvature tensor as a symmetric operator also denoted $Riem: \wedge^2\mathfrak{g} \to \wedge^2 \mfg$. From the additional $S^1$ invariance of our metric, we conclude that the eigenspaces of $K$ are $V_m := \{ \r \xi_1 \wedge \xi_2\}$ and $V_M = \{ \r \xi_1 \wedge \xi_3 + \r \xi_2 \wedge \xi_3\}$, and where the eigenvalues are given by the sectional curvatures $K(\xi_1\wedge\xi_2)$, $K(\xi_1, \xi_3) = K(\xi_2, \xi_3)$, respectively. It follows that $Riem(\xi_i, \xi_j) \xi_k = 0,$ if $i, j, k$ are distinct.
nodes.statement_short: The $S^1$ symmetry splits $\wedge^2\mfg$ into the eigenspaces $\r\xi_1\wedge\xi_2$ and $\r\xi_1\wedge\xi_3+\r\xi_2\wedge\xi_3$.
assumptions: From the additional $S^1$ invariance of our metric
conclusions: the eigenspaces of $K$ are $V_m := \{ \r \xi_1 \wedge \xi_2\}$ and $V_M = \{ \r \xi_1 \wedge \xi_3 + \r \xi_2 \wedge \xi_3\}$
$Riem(\xi_i, \xi_j) \xi_k = 0,$ if $i, j, k$ are distinct

nodes.name: Sectional curvature formula
nodes.statement: One calculates the sectional curvatures as follows: \begin{equation} K(\xi_i \wedge \xi_j) = \frac{(Riem(\xi_i, \xi_j) \xi_j, \xi_i)}{|\xi_i \wedge \xi_j|^2}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Curvature $Riem(\xi_2,\xi_1)\xi_1$ and $K(\xi_1 \wedge \xi_2) = 4-3\lambda$
nodes.statement: or, \begin{equation} Riem(\xi_2, \xi_1) \xi_1 = (1 - \frac34 \lambda) \xi_2. \end{equation} \vs and therefore \begin{equation} K(\xi_1 \wedge \xi_2) = \frac{(Riem(\xi_2, \xi_1) \xi_1, \xi_2)}{|\xi_1\wedge \xi_2|^2} = 16 \cdot (1- 3 \frac{\lambda}4) \cdot \frac14 = 4 - 3 \lambda. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The $\xi_1\wedge\xi_2$ sectional curvature equals $4-3\lambda$.

nodes.name: Remaining curvature components and $K(\xi_1\wedge\xi_3) = \lambda$
nodes.statement: Similar calculations show that \begin{equation} R(\xi_3, \xi_1) \xi_1 = \frac{\lambda}4 \xi_3. \end{equation} \begin{equation} Riem(\xi_1, \xi_3) \xi_3 = \frac{\lambda^2}4 \xi_1. \end{equation} \begin{equation} Riem(\xi_2, \xi_3) \xi_3 = \frac{\lambda^2}4 \xi_2. \end{equation} As a result, we get \begin{equation} K(\xi_1 \wedge \xi_3) = K(\xi_2 \wedge \xi_3) = \frac{\frac{\lambda^2}4}{\frac{\lambda}4} = \lambda. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The mixed sectional curvatures $K(\xi_1\wedge\xi_3)=K(\xi_2\wedge\xi_3)$ both equal $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Range of the sectional curvatures of $(S^3, g_A)$
nodes.statement: We conclude that the sectional curvatures of $S^3, g_A$ lie in $[\lambda, 4 - 3 \lambda]$, for $\lambda \in (0, 1]$, and they lie in $[4 - 3\lambda, \lambda]$, for $\lambda \geq 1$. Thus the sectional curvatures for $g_A$ are positive for $\lambda \leq \frac43$.
nodes.statement_short: Sectional curvatures lie between $\lambda$ and $4-3\lambda$, and stay positive iff $\lambda \leq 4/3$.
assumptions: for $\lambda \in (0, 1]$
for $\lambda \geq 1$
conclusions: the sectional curvatures of $S^3, g_A$ lie in $[\lambda, 4 - 3 \lambda]$, for $\lambda \in (0, 1]$, and they lie in $[4 - 3\lambda, \lambda]$, for $\lambda \geq 1$
the sectional curvatures for $g_A$ are positive for $\lambda \leq \frac43$

nodes.name: Jacobi operator $\mathcal{J}$
nodes.statement: In general, if $\gamma$ is a Riemannian geodesic with $\dot{\gamma} := T$, so that $\nabla_T T = 0$, the Jacobi operator $\mathcal{J}$ associates to a vectorfield $Y$ along $\gamma$ and normal to $\gamma$ the normal field along $\gamma$ given by \[ \mathcal{J}(Y) := \nabla_T^2 Y + Riem(Y, T) T. \]

nodes.name: The Jacobi operator $\mathcal{J}_1$ applied to $\xi_2$ and $\xi_3$
nodes.statement: We have, by equations (\ref{eqn:covder}, \ref{eqn:R12}), \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \mathcal{J}_1(\xi_2) & = & \nabla_{\xi_1}^2 \, \xi_2 + Riem(\xi_2, \xi_1) \, \xi_1 \\ & & \\ & = & \nabla_{\xi_1} \, \frac12 \xi_3 + (1 -\frac34 \, \lambda) \, \xi_2 \\ & & \\ & = & - \frac{\lambda}4 \xi_2\, + (1- \frac34 \, \lambda) \xi_2 \\ & & \\ & = & (1 - \lambda) \xi_2 \end{array} \] and so \begin{equation} \mathcal{J}_1(\xi_2) = (1 - \lambda) \, \xi_2, \end{equation} while \begin{equation} \mathcal{J}_1(\xi_3) = 0. \end{equation} since $\xi_3$, being tangent to the $S^1$ symmetry, is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{J}_1(\xi_2) = (1-\lambda)\xi_2$ and $\mathcal{J}_1(\xi_3)=0$.

nodes.name: Normal Jacobi field along $\gamma$
nodes.statement: A normal Jacobi field $Y$ along $\gamma$ is a field along $\gamma$ which may be written $Y =f\, \xi_2 + h \,\xi_3$ which satisfies $\mathcal{J}_1(Y) = 0$.

nodes.name: Coupled ODE system for a normal Jacobi field
nodes.statement: This gives us a $2 \times 2$ system of coupled ODEs, using (\ref{eqn:Jac12}, \ref{eqn:Jac13}), as well as (\ref{eqn:covder}) : \vs \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcl} f'' - \lambda h' + (1 - \lambda) \, f & = & 0 \\ & & \\ h'' + f' & = & 0. \end{array} \end{equation}

nodes.name: General solution of the Jacobi system
nodes.statement: Now use the first equation in (\ref{eqn:Jac1sys}) to solve for $\tilde{c} = \frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda} \, c$, to obtain, finally, \vs \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcl} f & = & a \cos t + b \sin t + c, \;\; \text{and} \\ && \\ h & = & b \cos t - a \sin t + \frac{1- \lambda}{\lambda} \, c \, t + d. \end{array} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $f = a\cos t + b\sin t + c$ and $h = b\cos t - a\sin t + \frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda}ct + d$.

nodes.name: Covering argument from local transitivity
nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lemma:action}, we know that $G_{\c}$ acts on $M_{\c}$. We will prove that it acts locally transitively at every point $v \in M_{\c}$. Assuming this for the moment, this proves that all orbits of $G_{\c}$ on $M_{\c}$ are open, and since $M_{\c}$ is connected, this proves that the mapping $A_v: G_{\c} \ni h \to h\cdot v \in M_{\c}$, for any fixed $v \in M_{\c}$, is surjective. Since $G_{\c}, M_{\c}$ are of the same complex dimension, and the map $A_v$ is $G_{\c}$ equivariant, Sard's theorem says that every point in $M_{\c}$ is a regular value of $A_v$, and hence, $A_v$ is a topological covering. If $v \in M$, the covering $A_v: G \to M$ is a diffeomorphism. Since the inclusions $G \subset G_{\c}, M \subset M_{\c}$ are homotopy equivalences, the covering $A_v$ has degree 1 over all of $M_{\c}$, and therefore $A_v$ is a global biholomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Granting local transitivity, orbits are open and $A_v$ is a degree-1 covering, hence a biholomorphism.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas

nodes.name: Reduce local transitivity to emptiness of the divisor $\mcp$
nodes.statement: To show that $G_{\c}$ acts locally transitively, it suffices to show that \[ DA_{v}: T^{1,0}_{I} G_{\c} = \mathfrak{g}_{\c} \to T_v^{1,0} M_{\c} \] is an isomorphism. This, in turn is equivalent to showing that, for a basis $\xi_1, \xi_2,\ldots, \xi_n$ of $\mathfrak{g}$ over $\r$, the complex fields $\tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_1, \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_2, \ldots, \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_n$ are a basis for $T^{1,0}M_{\c}$ over $\c$ at $v$. Define $\mcp = \{ \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_1 \wedge \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_2 \wedge \ldots \wedge \tilde{\xi}^{1,0}_n = 0\}$. We wish to show $\mcp$ is empty.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing the wedge-degeneracy locus $\mcp$ of the fields $\tilde\xi^{1,0}_i$ is empty.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas

nodes.name: Contradiction via Bishop disks and the maximum principle
nodes.statement: Assume it is not empty. Then $\mcp$ is a $G_{\c}$-invariant divisor on $M_{\c}$, and $\mcp \cap M = \emptyset$. Consider the plurisubharmonic function $u$ restricted to $\mcp$. Since $u$ is non-negative and proper when restricted to $\mcp$, it achieves a global minimum at some $v \in \mcp$. The map $A_v$ restricted to $G$ gives an embedding of $G$ into $\mcp \subset M_{\c}$ where it is a $CR$-submanifold of real dimension $n$. Note that the function $u$ is constant on $S_v := A_v(G)$. Since $\dim_{\c} \mcp < n$, $S_v$ cannot be a totally real submanifold in $\mcp$. Hence its complex tangent space is positive dimensional at every point. Its Levi-form cannot be trivial, since otherwise the leaves of the Levi foliation of $S_v$ would give positive-dimensional complex submanifolds in the level set $\{u = u(v)\}$, which is strictly pseudoconvex, by the tube construction. By a classical construction in complex analysis (local Bishop disks), there exists a continuous mapping $F: \bar{\triangle} \to U \subset M_{\c}$, where $U$ is a small polydisk neighborhood of $v$, and with $F|_{\triangle}$ holomorphic and non-constant, and $F(\partial \triangle) \subset S_v$. Thus $u\circ F|_{\partial\triangle} \equiv u(v)$. Therefore, $F(\triangle) \subset \mcp \cap U$, since $\mcp \cap U$ is closed and analytic in $U$, which gives us that $u\circ F(z) \geq u(v),$ for all $z \in \triangle$. By the maximum principle, $u\circ F$ is constant on $\triangle$, contradicting, again, the strict pseudoconvexity of $S_v$.
nodes.statement_short: Assuming $\mcp \neq \emptyset$, minimize $u$ on it and derive a contradiction with strict pseudoconvexity.
nodes.section: 2 Grauert Tubes and Some Simple Lemmas

nodes.name: Local definition and basic properties of $\Phi$
nodes.statement: This map is, at first, just defined in a neighborhood of the zero section $G$. It is real analytic, $G$-equivariant and sends a real geodesic $\gamma \subset G$ to the real points of the corresponding $g_{\c}$-geodesic.
nodes.statement_short: Start from $\Phi$ defined near the zero section: real analytic, $G$-equivariant, geodesic-preserving.

nodes.name: Biholomorphy along a single complexified geodesic
nodes.statement: Now if we consider $TG$ with its adapted complex structure, which we will momentarily call $J_T$, and we consider the complex submanifold $T\gamma \subset TM, J_T$, for $\gamma$ a $g$-geodesic, then $\Phi$ restricted to $i T\gamma$ maps it biholomorphically onto a neighborhood of $\gamma \subset \gamma_{\c} \subset G_{\c}$.
nodes.statement_short: On each $iT\gamma$ the map $\Phi$ is a biholomorphism onto a neighborhood of $\gamma$ in $\gamma_{\c}$.

nodes.name: Holomorphy of $\Phi$ from the foliation by geodesics
nodes.statement: Since this is true for all geodesics in $G, \Phi$ is holomorphic from $TM, J_T$ to $G_{\c}$.
nodes.statement_short: Since the geodesic leaves fill $TM$, $\Phi$ is holomorphic for $J_T$.

nodes.name: Global extension via $G_{\c}$-equivariance and lemma 2.2
nodes.statement: But then $\Phi$ is locally $G_{\c}$-equivariant, and is, locally near the zero section, the inverse of the action map from $G_{\c} \to TM, J_T,$ which is a global biholomorphism, by lemma \ref{lem:homogeneity}. Hence, $\Phi$ is globally defined by analytic extension, and is holomorphic. It embeds every $T\gamma \subset TM, J_T$ onto $\gamma_{\c} \subset G_{\c}$ biholomorphically.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\Phi$ with the inverse of the global action biholomorphism, so it extends analytically to all of $TG$.

nodes.name: Identities (1) and (2) from uniqueness for holomorphic ODEs
nodes.statement: (1) and (2) follow from the holomorphy of $\gamma_{\c}, Y^{\c}_w, \Gamma,$ and $W^{\c}_w$, and the uniqueness theorem for holomorphic ODE.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides are holomorphic solutions of the same ODE with the same data, so they agree.

nodes.name: Identity (3) from the definition of $\Phi$
nodes.statement: (3) is simply (\ref{eqn:DExpC}) taking into account the definition of $\Phi$ (\ref{eqn:Expdef}), and parts (1) and (2).
nodes.statement_short: Combine the holomorphic $DExp_{\c}$ formula with the definition of $\Phi$ and parts (1), (2).

nodes.name: Reduce to surjectivity of $DF$ for the map $F=(E,M)$
nodes.statement: It suffices to consider the map \[ F(x) := \left(\begin{array}{c} E(x) \\ \\ M(x) \end{array}\right) \] and show the differential is surjective for some $x \in \r^3$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the interior claim to finding a point where $D(E,M)$ is surjective.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Compute $DF$ and its $2\times 2$ minors
nodes.statement: But this differential is \[ DF(x) = \left(\begin{array}{ccc} 2\lambda_1 \, x_1 & 2\lambda_2 \, x_2 & 2\lambda_3 x_3 \\ & & \\ 2\lambda_1^2 \, x_1 & 2\lambda_2^2 \, x_2 & 2\lambda_3^2 \, x_3 \end{array} \right), \] whose minor determinants are (up to a factor of $\pm2$) \[ \begin{array}{l} \lambda_1 \, \lambda_2 \, (\lambda_2 - \lambda_1) \, x_1 \, x_2,\\ \\ \lambda_1 \, \lambda_3 \, (\lambda_3 - \lambda_1) \, x_1 \, x_3, \; \text{and}\\ \\ \lambda_2 \, \lambda_3 \, (\lambda_3 - \lambda_2) \, x_2 \, x_3. \end{array} \]
nodes.statement_short: Write down the Jacobian of $(E,M)$ and its three minor determinants.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Conclude maximal rank for non-zero coordinates
nodes.statement: Since we are assuming that not all $\lambda_i$ are equal, then choosing all $x_i$ non-zero will give maximal rank.
nodes.statement_short: Distinct eigenvalues plus all $x_i \neq 0$ make some minor non-zero.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Set up the Jacobian matrix $B$ and its vanishing minors
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be the two by four matrix \[ B = \left(\begin{array}{cccc} \lambda_1 z_1 & \lambda_2 \, z_2 & \lambda_3 \, z_3 & - a \, w \\ & & & \\ \lambda_1^2 \, z_1 & \lambda_2^2 \, z_2 & \lambda_3^2 \, z_3 & - b \, w \end{array} \right). \] We wish to show that there are no $(z_1, z_2, z_3, w) \neq (0,0,0,0)$ which solve (\ref{eqn:qe}) and (\ref{eqn:qm}), and for which the rank of $B$ is $<$ 2, or the six $2\times 2$ minors of $B$ are 0:
nodes.statement_short: Singular points of $C_{a,b}$ are where all six $2\times2$ minors of $B$ vanish.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Contradiction: at least two coordinates must be non-zero
nodes.statement: On the other hand, it is clear that any 4-tuple $(z_1, z_2, z_3, w)$ satisfying (\ref{eqn:qe}) or (\ref{eqn:qm}) must have at least two non-zero components, while on the other hand, all the constants in this last array of equations are non-zero under our assumptions. This is a contradiction, hence $C_{a,b}$ is smooth.
nodes.statement_short: Any point on either quadric has two non-zero coordinates, contradicting the vanishing minors.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Genus computation by adjunction
nodes.statement: To complete the proof, we use the classical genus formula \[ g(C_{a,b}) = 1 + \frac12 \; C_{a,b} \cdot (C_{a,b} + K_{\q_{E,a}}), \] where $K_{\q_{E,a}}$ is the canonical class of $\q_{E,a} \sim -2 H$, where $H$ in turn is the hyperplane section of $\q_{E,a} \subset \p^3$. Since $C_{a,b} \sim 2 H$, we see that $g(C) = 1$, as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the adjunction formula with $C_{a,b}\sim 2H$ and $K_{\q_{E,a}}\sim -2H$ to get genus 1.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Picard's theorem forces the velocity map to be constant
nodes.statement: Now the map $v: \c \to C_{a,b} \subset \p^3$ associated to a complexified geodesic with initial conditions $a = E(\gamma(0)), b = M(\gamma(0)),$ must actually map into the affine piece $C^{{aff}}_{a,b} = C_{a,b} \cap \mfg_{\c} = C_{a,b} \setminus C_{a,b} \cap \{w = 0\}$. But this last intersection is non-empty and a holomorphic map of $\c$ to $C^{aff}_{a,b}$ must factor through the universal covering $\pi: \mathbb{C} \to C_{a,b}$, but must omit the infinite set $\pi^{-1}(C_{a,b} \cap\{w = 0\})$. Thus, the map $c$ must be constant, by Picard's theorem.
nodes.statement_short: A holomorphic map $\c \to C^{aff}_{a,b}$ omitting an infinite set must be constant.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Constant velocity means geodesics are 1-parameter subgroups
nodes.statement: In real terms, this means that the real geodesic satisfies \[ \dot{\gamma} \equiv \xi \in \mfg, \] If we assume, without loss of generality, that $\gamma(0) = e \in G,$ this means that $\gamma(s)$ is the 1-parameter subgroup $\exp(s \xi)$ of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Constant $\dot\gamma$ in the left-invariant frame makes $\gamma$ a 1-parameter subgroup.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Propagate from a dense open set to all geodesics
nodes.statement: Now this conclusion holds true for all initial conditions $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_0$ in a dense open set of $\mfg = T_0G.$ By continuity of solution of ODEs, this must hold true for all geodesics passing through 0, and hence, by left translation, for all geodesics.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity in initial conditions plus left translation extends the conclusion to every geodesic.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Contradiction with distinctness of the $\lambda_i$
nodes.statement: However, it is well-known that any left invariant metric for which all geodesics through $e$ are 1-parameter subgroups is necessarily bi-invariant and hence round (see e.g. \cite{o}, ch. 11, Proposition 9). This would contradict our assumption that the $\lambda_i$ are all distinct.
nodes.statement_short: Such a metric would be bi-invariant and round, contradicting distinct eigenvalues.
nodes.section: 4 The Free Rigid Body and Complex Integrals

nodes.name: Invoke Sz\H{o}ke's result and identify the isometry group
nodes.statement: This is an immediate consequence of a result of Sz\H{o}ke \cite{s2} (cf also \cite{a1}). The metric (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) has an isometry group $G \times S^1$ where the factor $S^1$ acts by right multiplication on $G$ by the 1-parameter subgroup $e^{t\, \xi_3}$ on the right, i.e., by $R_{e^{t\, \xi_3}}$, periodic of period $2\pi$, and the factor $G$ acts by left multiplication $L_g$ on $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Cite Sz\H{o}ke's theorem and record that $g_A$ has isometry group $G \times S^1$.

nodes.name: Build the product manifold $G \times S^1$ with metric $g_{\mu}$
nodes.statement: Consider the manifold $G \times S^1$, where $G$ is given the bi-invariant metric of sectional curvature 1, which is the special case of (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) with $\lambda_1= 1$, and the $S^1$ factor is given the metric $\mu d\theta^2,$ where $d\theta^2$ is the invariant metric of length $2\pi$ on $S^1$ and $\mu$ is a real constant $> 0$. So $G\times S^1$ has the metric $g_{\mu}$ defined by \begin{equation} g_{\mu} = g_I \oplus \mu \, d\theta^2. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Equip $G\times S^1$ with the round metric plus $\mu\,d\theta^2$.

nodes.name: Form the $S^1$ quotient and its submersion metric
nodes.statement: Consider the quotient manifold of $G\times S^1$ by the action of $S^1 = \{e^{i t}\}$ on $G\times S^1$ given by $e^{i t} \cdot (g, e^{i \theta}) = (g\cdot e^{2 t\, \xi_3}, e^{i(\theta + t)}).$ Then it is easy to see that the quotient manifold $G\times S^1/\sim$ is diffeomorphic to $G$. Let $\bar{g}_{\mu}$ be the Riemannian submersion metric from (\ref{eqn:gmu}). By construction, this metric is invariant under left translation by $G$ and by right translation by $e^{- t \, \xi_3}$. Consequently, it is one of the left invariant metrics on $G$ with an extra isometric action from the right. It is an easy calculation to see which ones arise in this manner.
nodes.statement_short: Quotient by the diagonal circle action; the submersion metric is left-invariant on $G$.

nodes.name: Fix $A$ and normalize the metrics
nodes.statement: Let \begin{equation} A = \left(\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & & \\ & 1 & \\ & & \lambda \end{array}\right). \end{equation} Explicitly, we will normalize our metrics so that $g_A(\xi_1, \xi_1) = g_A(\xi_2, \xi_2) = \frac14,$ and $g_A(\xi_3, \xi_3) = \frac{\lambda}4$.\footnote{This means that instead of $g_A(\cdot,\cdot) = -B(A(\cdot), \cdot)$, we now have $g_A(\cdot, \cdot) = -\frac18 B(A(\cdot), \cdot)$.} With this normalization, the case $A = I$ gives the round metric with sectional curvature $K = 1$ on $G \cong S^3$.
nodes.statement_short: Pin down $A = \mathrm{diag}(1,1,\lambda)$ and the normalization making $A=I$ the round metric.

nodes.name: Compute the normal projection and identify $\lambda = \frac{\mu}{2+\mu}$
nodes.statement: We want to see which $\lambda$ in (\ref{eqn:U2sym}) will arise from Sz\H{o}ke's construction. Computing at $(e,1) \in G\times S^1$, the tangent vector to the $S^1$ action we will quotient by is given by $(2\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta})$. The projection of $(\xi_3, 0)$ onto this direction is given by \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcl} (\xi_3,0)^T & = & \frac{((\xi_3, 0), (\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}))}{|\xi_3 + \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}|^2} (\xi_3, \frac{\partial \;\;}{\partial \theta}), \\ & & \\ & = & \frac2{2+\mu} (\xi_3, \dbdth) \end{array} \end{equation} and hence the normal component is given by \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcl} (\xi_3,0)^N & = & (\xi_3,0) - (\xi_3,0)^T \\ & & \\ & = & (\frac{\mu}{2+\mu} \xi_3, \frac2{2+\mu} \dbdth). \end{array} \end{equation} Thus, \[ |\xi_3^N|^2 = 2 \frac{\mu}{2+\mu}, \] which means that the quotient metric on $G$ is $g_A$ with $A$ in (\ref{eqn:A}) having $\lambda = \frac{\mu}{2 + \mu}.$ Hence, any $\lambda \in (0, 1)$ appears. The limit case $\mu = +\infty$ is just the case of the round sphere, $\lambda = 1$, which also has an entire tube, of course.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $|\xi_3^N|^2$ to get $\lambda = \mu/(2+\mu)$, covering all of $(0,1)$, with $\lambda=1$ the round case.

nodes.name: Reduce to entirety of the complexified geodesic
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma$ be the real geodesic on $G$ with initial conditions $\gamma(0) = e \in G$ and $\dot{\gamma}(0) = v_0 \in T_eG \cong \mfg$. We solve the geodesic equations (\ref{eqn:geodeqns1}) in the appendix \cite{web} relatively explicitly to show that the complexified geodesic $\gamma_{\c}(\zeta)$ is an entire function from $\c$ to $G_{\c}$. The other statements in the proposition follow from smooth dependence on initial conditions.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to show $\gamma_{\c}$ is entire; the rest follows from smooth dependence on data.

nodes.name: Recall the geodesic equations for $A = \mathrm{diag}(1,1,\lambda)$
nodes.statement: For convenience, we repeat here the equations (\ref{eqn:geodeqns1}) from \cite{web} for the tangent vector $T = a\, \xi_1+b\, \xi_2+c\, \xi_3$ to a geodesic, subject to the initial condition $T(0) = a_0 \, \xi_1+ b_0\, \xi_2 +c_0 \, \xi_3,$ for a metric of the form $g_A$, with $A$ as in (\ref{eqn:A}): \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \dot{a} & = & -b\, c\, (\lambda - 1) \\ &&\\ \dot{b} & = & - a\, c\, (1 - \lambda) \\ &&\\ \dot{c} & = & 0, \end{array} \] where $\dot{a} = T(a)$, etc.
nodes.statement_short: Quote the reduced Euler equations for the tangent vector $T$.

nodes.name: Solve the reduced linear system for $a$ and $b$
nodes.statement:
We get that $c \equiv c_0 \in $, and the system reduces to \[  egin{array}{rcr} \dot{a} & = & -
u\, b \ &&\ \dot{b} & = & 
u \, a, \end{array} \] with $

nodes.statement_short: With $c \equiv c_0$ the pair $(a,b)$ rotates at rate $\nu = c_0(\lambda-1)$.

nodes.name: Complexify: $T_{\c}$ is an entire $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\c)$-valued function
nodes.statement: Set \[ T_{\c} = a(\zeta) \, \xi_{1,\c} +b(\zeta) \, \xi_{2,\c} + c_0 \, \xi_{3,\c}, \] which is an entire function from $\c \to \mathfrak{sl}(2,\c) \subset \c^4.$
nodes.statement_short: The trigonometric solution extends to an entire Lie-algebra-valued function of $\zeta$.

nodes.name: Linear ODE with entire coefficients has entire solutions
nodes.statement: Considering $\gamma_{\c}$ as a function from, at first, a neighborhood of $\r \subset \c$ to $G_{\c} = SL(2,\c) \subset \c^4$, we have that it satisfies the equation \[ \gamma_{\c}(\zeta)^{-1} \cdot \dot{\gamma_{\c}} = T_{\c}, \] where $\dot{\gamma}_{\c} = \frac{d\;\;}{d \zeta}$, since we are using the left-invariant parallelism to trivialize $T^{1,0}G_{\c}$. Equivalently, we have \[ \dot{\gamma}_{\c} = \gamma_{\c} \cdot T_{\c}, \] which is a linear equation, with $T_{\c}$ entire and known, on all of $\c$. Hence all its solutions extend to entire functions, proving the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: $\dot\gamma_{\c} = \gamma_{\c}T_{\c}$ is linear with entire $T_{\c}$, so all solutions are entire.

nodes.name: Reduce to the rank criterion of the rank lemma
nodes.statement: By lemma \ref{lem:rankDPhi}, to find singularities of $D\Phi$ at points $t v \in T_eG$, it suffices to
nodes.statement_short: Use the rank formula to turn singularity detection into a four-step computation.

nodes.name: Plan step 1: solve the Jacobi equation along $\gamma$
nodes.statement: Solve the Jacobi equation $\mathcal{J}_1(Y) = 0, Y = f \,\xi_2 + h\, \xi_3,$ along $\gamma$, the geodesic in $G$ with initial condition $\gamma(0) = e \in G$, and $\dot{\gamma}(0) = \xi_1 \in T_eG \cong \mfg$.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: solve $\mathcal{J}_1(Y)=0$ along the geodesic with $\dot\gamma(0)=\xi_1$.

nodes.name: Plan step 2: fix the initial conditions for $Y_2, Y_3$
nodes.statement: Set $Y_i = f_i\, \xi_2 + h_i \, \xi_3, i =2, 3,$ where $f_i(0) = h_i(0) = 0,$ and \vs \begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2'(0)& h_2'(0) \\& \\f_3'(0) & h_3'(0) \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 0 \\& \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Plan: normalize the Jacobi fields by an identity matrix of first derivatives at $0$.

nodes.name: Plan step 3: re-express in the right-invariant frame
nodes.statement_short: Plan: pass to the $\eta^{1,0}$ frame.

nodes.name: Plan step 4: evaluate and solve $\Delta(t) = 0$
nodes.statement: Evaluate \[\Delta(t) = \det Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \beta_2(i t) \\ & \\ \alpha_3(i t) & \beta_3(i t) \end{array} \right).\] Solve $\Delta(t) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: the singularities are the zeros of $\det \mathrm{Im}$ of the coefficient matrix at $it$.

nodes.name: State the target: a unique positive root
nodes.statement: We will show that $\Delta(t) = 0$ has a unique root $t_*(\lambda) \in (0, +\infty)$, proving the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Announce that $\Delta$ has exactly one positive root $t_*(\lambda)$.

nodes.name: Execute step 1: quote the Jacobi solution from the appendix
nodes.statement: Step (1) is calculated in section \ref{sub:JacA}, (\ref{eqn:Jac1soln}): \[ \begin{array}{rcl} f & = & a \cos t + b \sin t + c\\&&\\h & = & b \cos t - a \sin t + \frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda} c t + d, \end{array} \] where $a, b, c ,d \in \r$.
nodes.statement_short: Import the general solution $f,h$ of the Jacobi system from the appendix.

nodes.name: Execute step 2: impose the initial conditions
nodes.statement: (2) says, first, that $c = - a, d = - b,$ and further the first order initial conditions say \vs \[ \begin{array}{rcccl} f'_2(0) & = & b & =& 1 \\&&&&\\h'_2(0) & =& - \frac{a}{\lambda} & = & 0\end{array} \] \vs and \vs \[ \begin{array}{rcccl}f'_3(0) & = & b & = & 0\\ &&&&\\ h'_3(0) & = & - \frac{a}{\lambda} & =& 1.\end{array} \] \vs Hence, in the basis $\xi_2, \xi_3$ for normal fields to $\gamma$, we have \vs \begin{equation} \left(\begin{array}{cc} f_2 & f_3 \\&\\ h_2 & h_3 \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\ \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The initial conditions give the explicit $2\times 2$ matrix of $f_i, h_i$.

nodes.name: Execute step 3: change to the $\eta$ frame and take imaginary parts
nodes.statement: As to step (3), as in $(\ref{eqn:xi2eta})$ we have at $g \in \exp t \xi_1$ the change of basis from the $\xi$'s to the $\eta$'s is given by the action $Ad(- t \xi_1)$, explicitly: \vs \[ \begin{array}{rcccl} \eta_2 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \, \xi_2 & = & \cos t \; \xi_2 + \sin t \; \xi_3, \\ &&&&\\ \eta_3 & = & Ad(\exp(- t \xi_1)) \xi_3 & = & - \sin t \; \xi_2 + \cos t \; \xi_3. \end{array} \] \vs so that we have \vs \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2 & \alpha_3\\ & \\ \beta_2 & \beta_3 \end{array}\right) & = & \left( \begin{array}{cc} \cos t & - \sin t \\& \\ \sin t & \cos t \end{array}\right) \cdot \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & - \lambda (\cos t - 1) \\&\\ \cos t - 1& \lambda \sin t + (1 - \lambda) t \end{array}\right) \\ && \\ & = & \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sin t & \lambda [(\cos t - 1) + \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \sin t] \\ & \\ - (\cos t -1) & \lambda [\sin t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cos t] \end{array}\right). \end{array} \] \vs It follows directly that \vs \[ Im \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha_2(i t) & \alpha_3(i t) \\ & \\ \beta_2(i t) & \beta_3(i t)\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} \sinh t & 0 \\ & \\ 0 & \lambda [\sinh t - \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t \cosh t] \end{array}\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Rotating by $Ad(\exp(-t\xi_1))$ and substituting $t \to it$ diagonalizes the imaginary part.

nodes.name: Execute step 4: unique positive root of $\frac{\lambda-1}{\lambda}t=\tanh t$
nodes.statement: Finally, we have $\Delta(t) = 0$ if and only if \vs \begin{equation} \frac{\lambda - 1}{\lambda} \, t = \tanh t. \end{equation} \vs It is clear pictorially or from an elementary calculus computation that, if $\lambda >1$, there is a unique $t_*(\lambda) > 0$ satisfying (\ref{eqn:tstar}), as claimed
nodes.statement_short: The determinant vanishes exactly at the unique positive solution of $\frac{\lambda-1}{\lambda}t=\tanh t$.
